judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 95, which pays for suicide prevention aimed at veterans and serving military members. It sets aside $300,000 for the two years starting July 2025, for grants run by the state health department. The money must go to work with the federal veterans department, to setting standards for spotting who is at risk, and to training people who take that first call. It must also train more peer supporters, improve handover between military and civilian care, and fund a statewide campaign on storing firearms and medicines safely. The programme ends in June 2027. The Montana Senate passed it 39-11, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 110, which tightens safety rules for amusement rides such as fairground rides. Every ride must be inspected at least once every 12 months by a qualified inspector, and the act defines who counts as one. A ride may not be run for the public unless that inspector has issued a certificate. The operator must carry liability insurance of at least $500,000 for the injury or death of one person, and at least $1 million for one incident. Riders are also given clearer duties of their own. The Montana Senate passed it 33-16, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 181, which strengthens Montana's Indian Education for All programme. Schools must consult tribes, and the act sets out the role of Indian language and cultural specialists. The Office of Public Instruction must report each year to two legislative committees on how the money is used. A school district that does not file its yearly report loses the full Indian Education for All payment until it does. A district that files a report failing to show the money went to the right purposes has its funding cut for the next year. The Montana House passed it 69-28, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 182, which loosens the rules for Montana's Indian language programme. The programme helps tribes keep their languages alive. Tribes now get more freedom in how they set up the partnerships it runs on. The act also pushes the programme to join up with the Indian language classes that school districts already run, so the two are not kept apart. It asks teachers and tribal staff to train together. The stated aim is to help keep American Indian culture strong, as the Montana constitution requires. The Montana Senate passed it 35-13, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 276, which changes what a voter must show at the polls. The card must now be current, valid and easy to read. A student photo card from the Montana university system, or from a school in one named national sports association, now counts on its own. A school district card no longer counts as the photo part of the back-up option. The act also ends the route that let a voter who could not meet the rules sign a note giving the reason and cast a provisional ballot. The Montana House passed it 57-42, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 457, which gives the legislature teeth when someone ignores a subpoena. A subpoena is an order to appear or to hand over records. If a person does not comply, the chamber that issued it may vote to hold them in contempt. When the legislature is not sitting, members may be polled by post instead. A person convicted of criminal contempt of the legislature faces a fine of up to $1,000, up to 12 months in county jail, or both. The Montana House passed it 55-44, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 492, which narrows what elected state officials must disclose about their business interests. Officials, candidates for statewide or district office, and department directors file a yearly business disclosure statement. They used to have to list every business in which they held any interest at all. Now they list only those where they hold more than 10 percent, or more than 1 percent if the company is publicly traded. The same 10 percent floor now applies to land they must report, other than their own home. The Montana House passed it 56-43, and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 560, which asks what a nonprofit hospital gives back for the property tax it does not pay. A nonprofit hospital pays no property tax. Each one must now report to the state health department what it spends on free care and other help to the community. It uses the figures it already sends to the federal tax office each year. That yearly total must be more than the property tax it would have owed. The revenue department works out that tax figure. A hospital that falls short pays a fee, and that money goes to a new fund for small rural hospitals. The Montana House passed it 72-28, and it became law.
